factCheck.claim: On 3 June 2015 floodwaters carrying fuel reached a filling station at Kwame Nkrumah Circle where people had taken shelter, and the station exploded; estimates of the dead range from about 150 to more than 250; the split between flood and fire is uncertain; the day is now National Flood Disaster Day; flooding in 2025 and 2026 recurred.
factCheck.explanation: From a JoyNews feature on Accra’s flooding history, which flags the uncertain figures and says 132.2 mm of rain in May 2025 killed four people.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Accra under water again: inside Ghana’s 66-year flooding crisis that nobody has fixed”.

factCheck.claim: A May 2025 rain of 132.2 mm killed five people and displaced more than 3,000; the 2015 fire killed over 150 people; June 3 is National Flood Disaster Day.
factCheck.explanation: From an opinion article by an environmental policy lecturer, which differs from another source on the 2025 death toll (four or five).

Check against named sources: Public Health Act 2012 (Act 851) section 56 offence; the Lapaz case in 2017 (21 people fined GH¢720 each or six months in jail); cholera June 2014 to February 2015 (over 20,500 cases, 121 deaths; breakdown in waste management); World Bank flood-loss estimate (not used here).
Have a pastor, an imam and a traditional leader review the faith paragraph (Genesis 2:15; Deuteronomy 23:12 to 14; the saying that cleanliness is half of faith; Qur’an 7:56; Leviticus 19:18).
The fines mentioned are from 2017 and may have changed; the story says so. Check current rules with the Environmental Health service.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about giving children true, many-sided reasons for a good habit. It shows an educated person who litters and an unschooled elder who keeps her street clean, and it breaks the idea that care for the environment depends on certificates.

teacherGuide.overview: A science story that introduces turbidity, links galamsey to muddy rivers and water supply, and shows that prevention beats cure. It teaches careful reading of figures that differ.
learningGoals: Explain turbidity and how it is measured.
Describe how muddy rivers affect water plants, fish and people.

beforeReading: Fill two jars, one with clean water and one with muddy water, and ask learners which is safe to drink and why.
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to compare 500 with 5,000 and 12,000.
afterReading: Make a bottle filter as a demonstration. Do not drink the water.

discussion: Why do figures sometimes differ between reports?
What can a community do to protect its river banks?
reflection: What would you like your river to look like in twenty years?

mathsExtension.task: Normal water is up to 500 NTU. A river has 5,000 NTU. How many times higher is it?

teacherGuide.overview: A science story about mercury and how it moves. It teaches bioaccumulation and the difference between evidence, warnings and speculation, and it shows safer alternatives.
learningGoals: Describe how mercury is used to catch gold and where it goes.
Explain bioaccumulation with a food chain.
Separate what is shown by studies from what is warned.
beforeReading: Tell learners the lesson is for understanding and that no one should handle or test mercury.
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to sort statements into Shown / Warned / Not known.
afterReading: Draw a food chain showing how a metal builds up.
List three questions to ask a health worker.
discussion: Why can we not clean up a poison simply by washing it away?
How should we act when evidence is incomplete but a risk is serious?
reflection: What would make gold mining safer for the people who live near it?

mathsExtension.task: In a food chain, a substance doubles at each of four steps. If it starts at 1 unit, how much is there at the end?

factCheck.claim: Miners mix mercury with ore to form an amalgam and burn off the mercury; mercury damages the nervous system, kidneys and heart; children are especially vulnerable; vapour is inhaled, including at home; mercury was legal and sold openly in shops (2014); contaminated wastewater pollutes rivers and fish.

factCheck.reference: Human Rights Watch, “Mercury: Ghana’s poisonous problem” (10 October 2014).

factCheck.claim: Heavy metals (lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic) consistently found in placentas from mothers in galamsey areas; a birth-outcomes analysis of 75 deceased mother-infant pairs (2021 to 2024) across five regions; kidney harm in children is suspected from adult data, not proven; DNA effects are a warning.
factCheck.explanation: From a report of a Paediatric Society workshop. The article separates reported findings from warnings.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Exposure to galamsey-linked pollution could trigger acute kidney disease: Pediatric Society” (9 February 2026).

teacherGuide.overview: A story about a child pulled from school by poverty and mining. It teaches the law on child labour, the real dangers, and how families, teachers and officers can work together.
learningGoals: Explain why a child might leave school for mining.
Name the laws that protect children from dangerous work.
Describe ways schools and communities can help children return.
beforeReading: Tell learners the story is about a hard topic and that some may know children like Poku. Remind them to speak kindly.
whileReading: At page 5, ask why numbers differ and why an undercount is possible.
afterReading: Role-play a kind conversation between a friend and a classmate who has left school.
List who can help a child in danger, and how to contact them locally.
discussion: Why is it not enough to tell a child to go back to school?
What can friends do?
reflection: What would you want a friend to do if you were in Poku’s position?

mathsExtension.task: A day at the pit pays GH¢100 and a mother earns GH¢60 in a week. How many times more does the pit pay for one day than the mother earns in a week? (Numbers are invented for practice.)

support: Provide a chart of people who can help: teacher, welfare officer, elder, health worker.
stretch: Research how a community in another country reduced child labour.

culturalNotes: Poku, Rashida and Mrs Osafo are invented. The story treats child labour with care, avoids graphic detail and does not blame children or poor families.

The grant, loan, school feeding and job in the story are examples of support; availability differs by district. Check local services.
localiseThis: Invite a social welfare officer or a child protection volunteer; learn the local reporting number.

whatWeKnow: Thousands of Ghanaian children are involved in mining-related work, and laws protect them.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact number of children involved, which official and NGO counts give differently.

factCheck.claim: A 2022 UNICEF report estimates 20,000 to 30,000 children in mining-related activities; the Minerals Commission counts more than 5,600 directly involved (the forum said likely an undercount); many are 12 to 17, some as young as five; hazards include mercury and cyanide; girls face dropout, early pregnancy, sexual violence and trafficking; laws include Children’s Act (560), Labour Act (651), Human Trafficking Act (694) and ILO Convention 182; enforcement is weak.
factCheck.explanation: From a report of a National NGO Forum, with figures as reported there.
factCheck.reference: Ghanaian Times, “Poisoned playgrounds: National NGO forum demands urgent action to end child labour in galamsey” (1 August 2025).

teacherGuide.overview: A story about moral leadership and the idea of custodianship. It shows how one decision involves many voices and how law, tradition and young people’s evidence can support a leader’s choice.
learningGoals: Explain the idea of custodianship of land and water.
Weigh arguments for and against accepting payments from illegal miners.
Describe legal and community ways to protect a river.
beforeReading: Ask: what does it mean to look after something that does not belong only to you?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners which argument they find strongest and why.
afterReading: Role-play the night with each character’s views.
Draft a bylaw to protect a river.
discussion: Why is Kwaw’s question important?
How can a community give young people another route to income?
reflection: What would you do if offered a lot of money to harm something that lasts?

mathsExtension.task: The law punishes mining in forest reserves with 15 to 25 years in prison. What is the range?
If a bylaw plants 50 trees a week for 12 weeks, how many trees is that?

support: Provide role cards with each character’s main argument.
stretch: Research how other communities have protected sacred groves or rivers.

culturalNotes: The chief, queen mother, town and characters are invented. The story does not accuse any real chief or town.
The National House of Chiefs’ statement and the law described are from published reports. The idea that some chiefs profit is described as a reported claim, not a fact about any named chief.
Chieftaincy customs differ by area; adapt the setting and titles with local advice.
localiseThis: Use local titles, customs and a local river; invite a traditional leader or assembly staff member.

whatWeKnow: The National House of Chiefs says chiefs oppose galamsey and should be involved.
Mining in forest reserves is now banned by law.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How widely traditional leaders are involved in illegal mining, which reports describe differently.

factCheck.claim: The National House of Chiefs’ president said chiefs have consistently opposed galamsey but the current approach has not achieved the desired results; called for involving traditional authorities; chiefs are custodians of the land; polluted rivers and contaminated soils affect drinking water and food security; medical professionals warned that staple crops are affected by chemicals.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana News Agency report of 18 December 2025.
factCheck.reference: Ghana News Agency, “National House of Chiefs calls for stronger role of traditional authorities in galamsey fight”.

factCheck.claim: Mining in forest reserves is prohibited; penalties of 15 to 25 years’ imprisonment; aiding and abetting carries the same range; the revocation instrument became law on 10 December 2025.
factCheck.explanation: From a MyJoyOnline report of 18 December 2025.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Govt bans mining in forest reserves; violators face up to 25 years in prison”.

factCheck.claim: Some chiefs earn more from informal deals with machine owners than from formal royalties (an opinion claim); complicity by chiefs, assembly members and security officers is cited as a cause in an editorial.
factCheck.explanation: These are claims from opinion pieces and are not proven about any named person.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Why Ghana cannot defeat galamsey” (opinion); Graphic Online, “Can Ghana heal her water?” (editorial).

teacherGuide.overview: A role-play story that teaches how a law is made, read and tested. It shows the gap between a law on paper and a law in practice, and how licensing, data and prosecutions fit together.
learningGoals: Summarise the main provisions of the law on mining in forest reserves.
Explain why enforcement and licensing matter as much as the text of a law.
Take part in a respectful mock debate.
beforeReading: Assign roles: Speaker, Minister, Assembly Members, miner, lawyer, journalist, farmer, chief. Give each a short card with facts.
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to list what is a fact, what is an allegation and what is an opinion.
afterReading: Write a short speech for your role.
Make a chart: Law / Who enforces / What may go wrong / What would help.
discussion: Why can a strong law fail to protect rivers?
Why might a slow licence process push people to mine illegally?
reflection: What would a fair, workable law on small-scale mining look like?

mathsExtension.task: The penalty range for mining in forest reserves is 15 to 25 years. What is the middle of the range?

support: Provide role cards with key facts and sentence starters.
stretch: Compare Ghana’s mining laws with another country’s and discuss differences.

culturalNotes: The pupils, the lawyer and the teacher are invented. The laws are described from published reports; teachers should check current legislation.

This story is for classroom role-play and does not take a political party’s side.
localiseThis: Invite an Assembly Member, a lawyer or a clerk to judge the debate.
Check current laws before using the facts.

whatWeKnow: Mining in forest reserves has been banned by law since December 2025, with heavy penalties.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How well the law is enforced and whether prosecutions reach financiers and officials.

factCheck.claim: Mining in forest reserves is prohibited; 15 to 25 years’ imprisonment and 10,000 to 15,000 penalty units; foreigners 20 to 25 years and 100,000 to 300,000 penalty units; aiding and abetting 15 to 25 years; the Minerals and Mining (Amendment) Act 2019 (Act 995) applies; L.I. 2462 revoked, the instrument becoming law on 10 December 2025.
factCheck.explanation: From a MyJoyOnline report of 18 December 2025.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Govt bans mining in forest reserves; violators face up to 25 years in prison”.

factCheck.claim: Arrests outnumber convictions, cases stall, equipment disappears (allegations); licensing is slow and costly; recommended fast, decentralised licensing, mercury-free processing, prosecutions that reach financiers and officials, and alternative livelihoods.
factCheck.explanation: From an opinion piece by a researcher; some quotes in it are composites. It is opinion, not proof.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Why Ghana cannot defeat galamsey” (opinion, Dr Ebo Botchway).

factCheck.claim: Recommendations include publishing monthly turbidity and heavy metal levels for major rivers and enforcing the law against financiers.

teacherGuide.overview: A media-literacy story that shows how a radio club reports a contested issue fairly. It teaches the difference between facts, claims and opinions, how to protect sources and stay safe, and how civil society uses its voice peacefully.
learningGoals: Sort statements into facts, claims and opinions.
Explain the role of journalists, scientists and civil society in a public debate.
Plan a short fair report on a local issue.
beforeReading: Ask: where do you get news? How do you know if it is true?
whileReading: At page 7, ask learners to sort ten sentences from the story into three columns.
afterReading: Record a two-minute report on a local issue, with one fact, one claim and one opinion, clearly labelled.
Write three safe interview questions.
discussion: Why do reporters tell more than one side of a story?
How can we disagree and still be kind?
reflection: What is one question you would ask a leader in your community?

mathsExtension.task: About 54 people were arrested and 39 were taken to court. How many were not taken to court?

support: Give learners sentence cards to place into Facts, Claims and Opinions.
stretch: Compare how two news outlets report the same event and note differences.

whatWeKnow: A prayer walk and protests against galamsey took place in 2024, with different accounts of some events.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The full facts of the September 2024 arrests, which reports describe differently.

factCheck.claim: On 11 October 2024, the Bishops of the Accra Archdiocese and thousands of parishioners held an Environmental Prayer Walk; a petition went to the presidency; FixTheCountry and Democracy Hub joined; a priest said the fight belongs to everyone.

factCheck.reference: Africanews, “Ghana: Catholic Church takes stand against illegal mining, also known as galamsey”.

factCheck.claim: A #StopGalamseyNow protest planned for 21 to 23 September 2024 was blocked by a High Court injunction; about 54 people were arrested; 39 were arraigned and remanded for 12 days; lawyers and relatives alleged denial of food, counsel and visits, which police denied; the Ghana Journalists Association and MFWA called for rights to be respected.
factCheck.explanation: From the Media Foundation for West Africa’s account of 3 October 2024. Accounts differ.
factCheck.reference: MFWA, “#StopGalamseyNow: 53 anti-illegal mining protesters arrested”.

factCheck.claim: Heavy metals found in placentas from mothers in galamsey areas; kidney harm in children is suspected from adult data and not proven.

teacherGuide.overview: A closing story that imagines two futures for a river and asks every role to make a promise. It teaches that change needs a shared effort, that promises must be specific, and that children can lead by example.
learningGoals: Describe two possible futures for a river and what makes each one happen.
Write specific promises for different roles.
Make and share a personal promise.
beforeReading: Ask: if you could see your river in twenty years, what would you hope to see?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to write one promise for a leader and one for themselves.
afterReading: Make a “promise wall” in class and revisit it each term.
Plant a tree and photograph it each year.
discussion: Why are specific promises better than slogans?
How can we keep each other to our promises?
reflection: What is one promise you will keep this month?

mathsExtension.task: Benewaa is 13. How old will she be in 20 years?
A class plants one tree each year for 20 years. How many trees is that?

support: Give sentence starters: “I will… by…”.
stretch: Choose a local river or stream and write a ten-year restoration plan.

culturalNotes: The pupils and teacher are invented. The two futures are imagined by the characters and are not predictions.
The Rhine and Singapore River are used as examples that rivers can recover, not as models to copy exactly.
Every role in the story has a promise, so that no group is made the only villain or the only hero.
localiseThis: Use your own river and local leaders; invite a leader to read the promises and respond.

whatWeKnow: Rivers can recover when people decide to heal them, but it takes years.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How long it will take Ghana’s rivers, and which actions matter most.

factCheck.claim: Recovery may take 10 to 20 years of consistent work (an estimate); the Rhine was declared biologically dead in the 1970s and now supports life after investment and enforcement; recommended a Water Restoration Fund, river-by-river restoration plans, monthly public data and enforcement against financiers.
factCheck.explanation: From a Daily Graphic editorial, which is opinion; the Rhine claim should be confirmed with a river-science source.
factCheck.reference: Graphic Online, “Can Ghana heal her water?” (12 August 2026).

factCheck.claim: The Singapore River clean-up took about ten years (1977 to 1987).
factCheck.explanation: From the National Library Board Singapore’s encyclopedia entry.
factCheck.reference: NLB Singapore, Infopedia, “Cleaning of the Singapore River”.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about pride, honesty and teamwork in a crowded settlement. It models a summary in the learner’s own words and teaches fair play over reward.
learningGoals: Describe a settlement community’s strengths and struggles without stereotypes.
Explain why honesty matters even when rewards are tempting.
Write a summary using own words and main points only.
beforeReading: Ask: what do people say about places like Lagoon Side? What do the residents say?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners what they would do at the half-time offer.
afterReading: Write a three-sentence summary of the story in your own words.
Role-play telling a trusted adult about an unfair offer.
discussion: Why do labels hurt a community?
How can a team keep its name when it loses?
reflection: What would you do if someone offered you a reward to cheat?

mathsExtension.task: Caleb saved 4 of 5 shots. What percentage did he save?
A cup has 8 teams in a knockout. How many matches are played in total?

support: Give learners a summary frame: Who? What happened? How did it end? Use three sentences.
stretch: Summarise a news article in sixty words.

culturalNotes: Lagoon Side, the team and all people are invented. The word “ghetto” is used by some Ghanaians for crowded low-income settlements; the story shows the term as an outsiders’ label and presents the community’s own strengths and struggles.
The story includes a match-fixing offer to teach honesty. It does not show gangs, drugs or violence. Teachers should be ready to discuss peer pressure and trusted adults.
The flood scene shows the safety rule that children keep away from flooded water, drains and the lagoon edge.
localiseThis: Use real local sports, local clubs and your community’s actual strengths. Involve learners from different neighbourhoods.

factCheck.claim: A good summary is short, in the writer’s own words, in complete sentences and the same tense, and contains only the main points.
factCheck.explanation: A standard summary-writing guideline in Ghanaian English teaching; check against the BECE marking scheme.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA English Language syllabus and WAEC BECE English chief examiners’ reports; verify wording.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about prejudice, evidence and friendship across communities on a stuck trotro. It teaches direct and reported speech.
learningGoals: Explain why evidence comes before accusation.
Convert simple sentences from direct to reported speech.

beforeReading: Ask: have you ever been blamed for something you did not do? How did it feel?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners what they would do if they were a passenger.
afterReading: Change ten direct-speech sentences from the story into reported speech.
Write a short dialogue between two students from different neighbourhoods.
discussion: Why do we sometimes blame the person who seems different?
How can a group search for evidence fairly?
reflection: What do you do when you see someone accused without proof?

mathsExtension.task: A fare is GH¢3. Four students pay with a GH¢20 note between them. How much change?

The false accusation is resolved by evidence, not by guesswork; it teaches learners to question stereotypes of street children.

culturalNotes: The students, teacher and father are invented. The facts come from published case studies: the Cheonggyecheon in Seoul was covered from the late 1950s, an elevated highway stood over it by 1971, demolition began in 2003 and the restored stream opened in October 2005. Reported costs, cooling and visitor numbers are from project summaries and should be treated as reported figures.
The story is honest that the restored stream is partly fed by pumped river and groundwater, and that businesses and drivers had real concerns.
The story does not say Accra should copy Seoul; it shows that big changes need plans, money, leaders and years.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

teacherGuide.overview: A story about a city that uncovered a buried stream, with honest costs and benefits. It teaches how to weigh a big decision and models a descriptive paragraph using the five senses.
learningGoals: Describe the costs and benefits of restoring a buried stream.
Explain why different people held different views.
Write a descriptive paragraph using at least three senses.
beforeReading: Ask: what is buried or covered in your town that people once used?
whileReading: At page 4, ask learners which concerns were fair.
afterReading: Write a descriptive paragraph about a place you love, using three senses.
Debate: should a city remove a busy road to restore a stream?
discussion: Who gains and who might lose from a big project like this?
Is a partly artificial stream still worth having?
reflection: What would you want to change in your town if you had a plan, a budget and ten years?

support: Provide a five-senses chart with sentence starters.
stretch: Write a short letter to your Assembly proposing the clean-up of one drain, with two reasons and one solution.

culturalNotes: The students, teacher and father are invented. The facts come from published case studies: the Cheonggyecheon in Seoul was covered from the late 1950s, an elevated highway stood over it by 1971, demolition began in 2003 and the restored stream opened in October 2005. Reported costs, cooling and visitor numbers are from project summaries and should be treated as reported figures.
The story is honest that the restored stream is partly fed by pumped river and groundwater, and that businesses and drivers had real concerns.
The story does not say Accra should copy Seoul; it shows that big changes need plans, money, leaders and years.
localiseThis: Use real local drains and streams; do not send learners near water; involve drainage or planning officers.

factCheck.claim: The Cheonggyecheon in Seoul was covered with concrete from the late 1950s, topped by an elevated highway by 1971; demolition began in 2003 and the restored stream opened in October 2005, at a reported cost of about US$380 million.
factCheck.explanation: From an Asian Development Bank-supported case study; benefit figures are reported, not independently verified here.
factCheck.reference: Development Asia, “Revitalizing a City by Reviving a Stream” (development.asia).

the-country-that-grew-its-forest-back.music: Warm, rustling forest sounds with a gentle guitar; a thoughtful tune at the debate (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The students, uncle and farm are invented. The Costa Rica facts come from a published analysis: forest cover was just over 20 per cent in the 1980s and is now over 50 per cent (some sources say over 60 per cent); a 1996 law bans land-use change in forests; since 1997 nearly a million hectares have been enrolled at some point in a payments-for-ecosystem-services scheme; payments have lost over half their real value; effectiveness, fairness and enforcement are debated.

the-woman-who-asked-for-trees.music: Gentle East African-style lyre and drums; a rising, hopeful theme (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Rita, Mr Ohene and the school are invented. Wangari Maathai (1940–2011) was a real public figure; the facts are from the Nobel Prize biography and other published sources: born in Nyeri, Kenya, in 1940; first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate (University of Nairobi, 1971); the Green Belt Movement planted trees with women’s groups; she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004 and died on 25 September 2011.

The small payment for each surviving seedling is from the Green Belt Movement’s own website (about US 10 cents, paid to nursery groups) and a YES! Magazine profile (a nominal amount, less than 10 US cents a tree); a figure of 4 Kenyan shillings was suggested in a review but not confirmed, so it is not used. Her Nobel lecture itself says only that the work creates employment.

The number of trees is shown as differing accounts (more than 20 million in the Nobel biography; more than 30 million in her 2004 Nobel lecture; more than 51 million in the Green Belt Movement’s 2011 annual report).

The quotation “plant seeds of peace” is checked against the text of her Nobel lecture (10 December 2004), where it describes people who protect the environment, promote democracy and defend human rights. The payment for surviving seedlings is also in the movement’s 2011 annual report (compensation for seedlings planted and surviving).
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check every date and fact against the Nobel Prize biography and Nobel lecture (nobelprize.org), including what women told Maathai in the 1970s and the payment-per-tree detail.
Check the quotation on page 5 against the Nobel lecture.
Check the biography-paragraph tip against the NaCCA English syllabus.

characters: Grace Sefa: a 14-year-old girl in a school uniform, holding a small glass bottle labelled “insulin”.

narrationPlan.voice: Curious girl’s voice for Grace; a kind, patient voice for Papa Jacob; a clear voice for Mr Enchill
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and gentle, slowing for the science (about 118 words per minute)

the-bacterium-in-the-insulin-bottle.music: Quiet laboratory hum with a soft piano; a wondering, rising theme at the big idea (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Grace, Papa Jacob and Mr Enchill are invented. The science facts are from published sources: before genetic engineering, insulin came from the pancreas of pigs and cows (about ten thousand pounds of pancreas for one pound of crystals in 1923); in 1973 researchers showed that genes can be moved between bacteria; the first human insulin made in bacteria was approved in 1982; a heat-stable enzyme from Yellowstone bacteria made PCR practical; artemisinin came from sweet wormwood and the 2015 Nobel committee estimated it saves over 100,000 lives a year in Africa.

The nibima (Cryptolepis sanguinolenta) lines report laboratory findings only; no human clinical trial result is claimed. The story warns that no one should replace proper malaria treatment with a plant.

The idea that “everything should be kept because we cannot know what will be useful” is shown as the precaution argument, with an honest note that most species will not become medicines and that there are other strong reasons to protect them.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have a biology teacher check the simplified description of how insulin is made with bacteria and how PCR works.
Check the separate penicillin example (Fleming, 1928; Penicillium mould killing nearby Staphylococcus bacteria) and the description of insulin as a key for cells with a reliable source.
Check that the diabetes details are accurate and respectful, that the story does not give medical advice, and that families affected by diabetes are not alarmed.

factCheck.claim: Human insulin made in bacteria was first achieved in 1978 by a Genentech and City of Hope team, and the first such medicine (Humulin) was approved in 1982; before that insulin came from the pancreas of pigs and cows.

factCheck.reference: NSF, “rDNA insulin” (nsf.gov/impacts/rdna-insulin).

factCheck.claim: A heat-stable enzyme (Taq) from a Yellowstone hot-spring bacterium was isolated about a decade after the 1964 discovery of the bacterium, and became the basis of PCR.
factCheck.explanation: From the US National Science Foundation’s account of PCR.
factCheck.reference: NSF, “polymerase chain reaction” (nsf.gov/impacts/polymerase-chain-reaction).

factCheck.claim: Artemisinin, from sweet wormwood, was discovered by Tu Youyou’s team after a search of ancient texts; she shared the 2015 Nobel Prize; the Nobel committee estimated over 100,000 lives saved each year in Africa; resistance has emerged in Southeast Asia.
factCheck.explanation: From a PBS NewsHour report on the 2015 prize.
factCheck.reference: PBS NewsHour, “Chinese herbal therapy for malaria wins part of Nobel Prize in medicine” (pbs.org/newshour).

the-monkeys-of-boabeng-fiema.music: Soft village drums with forest birdsong and leaf rustle; a quiet, respectful tune at the funeral scene (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Silas, Mr Darkwah and Madam Blay are invented. The Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary is a real community sanctuary in the Bono East Region of Ghana, where local custom has long protected monkeys. The details here (monkeys treated as sacred, burial with rites, about 700 monkeys, a small sanctuary of 192 hectares (about 1.9 square kilometres) inside a sacred grove of about 4.4 to 4.5 square kilometres, problems with feeding and poor roads) come from published descriptions and should be checked with the community.

Species names differ between sources (“Geoffroy’s pied colobus” and “white-thighed colobus”, Colobus vellerosus; Campbell’s mona monkey is also called Lowe’s mona monkey). Colobus counts for 2006 differ: about 241 (University of Ghana study, citing Wong and Sicotte 2006) and over 365 (Species Survival Commission page, citing the same authors), so the story gives no single figure; the split between colobus and mona monkeys is not confirmed, so the story gives only a total range. A Journal of Tropical Ecology census (1990 to 2020) reports colobus growth of about 252 per cent in the sanctuary itself; yearly totals such as 451 in 2020 are not in the abstract and are not used. Sanctuary area: a University of Ghana study (Attuquayefio and Gyampoh) describes a 192-hectare sanctuary within a 4.5 square kilometre sacred grove, which explains the 1.9 and 4.4 figures.
The story respects the belief and does not argue that it is only a story; it shows how custom and science can work together.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have the Boabeng-Fiema community, the sanctuary management or the Ghana Wildlife Division review the story for accuracy and respect, including the funeral rites and the numbers.
Check the species names and the population figure with a recent survey by the sanctuary or a university.
Check the dialogue-punctuation tip against the NaCCA English syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about a real Ghanaian example of traditional conservation, told with respect for belief, honest about problems and curious about science. It models correctly punctuated direct speech.
learningGoals: Explain how custom can protect wildlife.
Name two problems the sanctuary faces.
Punctuate direct speech correctly in a narrative.
beforeReading: Ask: are there animals, trees or places that your community protects by custom? Why?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners how to respect a belief while asking questions.
afterReading: Interview an elder about a custom that protects nature; write a narrative with dialogue.

discussion: Can belief and science both protect a forest?
How should tourism money be shared with the community?

support: Provide a dialogue frame with correct quotation marks and a checklist.

culturalNotes: Silas, Mr Darkwah and Madam Blay are invented. The Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary is a real community sanctuary in the Bono East Region of Ghana, where local custom has long protected monkeys. The details here (monkeys treated as sacred, burial with rites, about 700 monkeys, a small sanctuary of 192 hectares (about 1.9 square kilometres) inside a sacred grove of about 4.4 to 4.5 square kilometres, problems with feeding and poor roads) come from published descriptions and should be checked with the community.

Species names differ between sources (“Geoffroy’s pied colobus” and “white-thighed colobus”, Colobus vellerosus; Campbell’s mona monkey is also called Lowe’s mona monkey). Colobus counts for 2006 differ: about 241 (University of Ghana study, citing Wong and Sicotte 2006) and over 365 (Species Survival Commission page, citing the same authors), so the story gives no single figure; the split between colobus and mona monkeys is not confirmed, so the story gives only a total range. A Journal of Tropical Ecology census (1990 to 2020) reports colobus growth of about 252 per cent in the sanctuary itself; yearly totals such as 451 in 2020 are not in the abstract and are not used. Sanctuary area: a University of Ghana study (Attuquayefio and Gyampoh) describes a 192-hectare sanctuary within a 4.5 square kilometre sacred grove, which explains the 1.9 and 4.4 figures.
The story respects the belief and does not argue that it is only a story; it shows how custom and science can work together.
localiseThis: Use your own region’s customs and species. Follow community rules on visiting; never feed wild animals.

factCheck.claim: At Boabeng-Fiema in Ghana’s Bono East Region, monkeys have long been treated as sacred, are buried with rites when they die, and live in a 192-hectare sanctuary within a sacred grove of about 4.5 square kilometres, with an estimated 600 to 700 or more monkeys; feeding by people causes conflict and poor roads limit visitors.
factCheck.explanation: From a published description of the sanctuary; the figures are approximate and species names differ between sources.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary”; Oryx, “Boabeng-Fiema Monkey Sanctuary: an example of traditional conservation in Ghana” (cambridge.org). Verify with the sanctuary.

culturalNotes: Roland, Mrs Amoo, Marvin and the school are invented. Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

the-forest-that-feeds-the-rivers.music: Soft forest sounds with a thoughtful guitar; a clear, steady tune at the conclusion (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Nelson, Madam Sakyi, Victor, Mr Awuah and Mrs Ahiable are invented. The Atewa Range Forest Reserve is real and the debate is real, so the story attributes each claim by role and does not name any politician or company. No claim in the story should be taught as settled fact.

Facts from published sources: conservation groups say Atewa holds the headwaters of the Ayensu, Densu and Birim rivers, which supply more than five million people; Global Wildlife Conservation reports about 3,000 plant species and over 570 butterfly species; in September 2026 environmental groups said illegal mining had spread into the reserve and called for a national park; they estimate eco-tourism and agroforestry could bring over US$5 million a year and at least 3,000 jobs; the paramount chief of the area has been reported to oppose bauxite mining; the government has argued that bauxite mining could bring revenue and that new technology could limit damage.

Formal commercial bauxite mining remains contested and, as far as the writer knows, the reserve has not been upgraded to a national park, while illegal mining is reported as an active threat; in September 2026 the Forestry Commission and the national anti-illegal mining team (NAIMOS, Operation Green Shield) were reported to have made arrests; the operation was announced on 22 October 2026 and some reports say three suspects were arrested at its launch. On 2 November 2026 Adom reported an armed clash during the operation in the reserve (one suspected miner killed, four arrested); this is deliberately kept out of the story. These details may have changed; teachers should check recent news before use.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the current status of the Atewa bauxite plans and of illegal mining in the reserve with up-to-date news and official statements, and correct the story if it has changed.
Check every attributed claim, especially the five-million-people figure, the species counts and the tourism and jobs estimates, against the original reports.
Check that the story is balanced and that Victor is presented with dignity and not as a villain; ask a local youth-programme worker to review.

characters: Doris Dwomoh: a 14-year-old girl in a school uniform, carrying an exercise book.
Uncle Opare: a lean man in his forties in a faded shirt and rubber boots, hands rough from digging.
Mr Nunoo: the social studies teacher, in a shirt and tie, holding a printed copy of a law.
Five miners: five men of different ages sitting on a bench outside a house, with a notebook between them.

narrationPlan.voice: Thoughtful girl’s voice for Doris; a tired but hopeful voice for Uncle Opare; a clear teacher’s voice for Mr Nunoo
narrationPlan.pace: Steady and hopeful, slowing for the legal steps and the letter (about 118 words per minute)

the-six-who-pooled.music: Slow, warm highlife guitar with a steady drum; a lifting tune at the group meeting (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Doris, Uncle Opare, Mr Nunoo and the five miners are invented, and the town and letter address are invented. The story does not say or suggest that miners are bad people; many take risks because there are few other jobs, and the story treats Uncle Opare with dignity. Children are never shown in or near a pit.

Facts from published sources: a legal guide to small-scale licences says the applicant must be a Ghanaian citizen of at least 18 and registered with the Minerals Commission district office, that licences may go to cooperatives and companies, that the application is published in the gazette and chiefs are notified, and that the first term is up to five years; the Minerals Commission’s guide says small-scale operations cover up to 25 acres under section 82 of Act 703; the Gold Board Act, 2025 (Act 1140) makes gold trading without a licence an offence and sets the Gold Board as buyer from miners who are not large-scale; Cabinet approved rCOMSDEP in August 2025 to promote cooperatives with concessions, training and shared processing centres.
The published pages do not say how cooperatives are formed or who qualifies, so the story tells readers to ask. Rules and fees change; the story is not legal advice.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Have an officer of the Minerals Commission or a mining lawyer check the licence steps, the 25-acre and five-year figures and the eligibility statement against Act 703 and its amendments, because the legal guide was a summary.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about learning from other countries’ attempts to bring small-scale gold miners into the law. It shows successes and failures side by side and models an argumentative paragraph.
learningGoals: Describe one thing that helped and one thing that failed in another country.
Explain why a law alone does not solve a problem.
Write an argumentative paragraph with evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
beforeReading: Ask: what is the difference between borrowing an idea and copying a plan?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to sort each example into helped or fell short.
afterReading: Write an argumentative paragraph on a question such as: should a school have a compulsory tree-planting day?
Find one of the four countries on a map and note its continent.
discussion: Why might a rule that bans miners from cooperating cause problems?
What support do you think small miners need besides a licence?
reflection: When have you changed your mind after hearing both sides of a question?

support: Give an argument frame: Some people argue… However, others argue… Therefore, in my view…
stretch: Compare two of the four countries in a short report with a heading, an introduction, findings and a recommendation.

culturalNotes: Selikem, Mr Tsikata and the school are invented. The country facts come from a 2012 analysis of formalisation approaches in Ecuador, Mongolia, Peru, Tanzania and Uganda; it is more than a decade old, so the story labels the date and tells learners not to assume the same figures today.
The story shows both what helped and what failed and says no country has fixed the problem completely. It does not name any politician, company or community.

factCheck.claim: A 2012 analysis found that Peru’s 2002 law set clear categories, lower fees and simpler environmental permits for small and artisanal miners, but the promotion policy never fully materialised, a minimum annual production applied and artisanal miners could not contract with each other; the cooperative SOTRAMI was Fairmined certified with a premium of 10 to 15 per cent.
factCheck.explanation: From a 2012 analysis of formalisation in five countries; dated.
factCheck.reference: Hinton, J. (2012), “Analysis of formalization approaches in the artisanal and small-scale gold mining sector based on experiences in Ecuador, Mongolia, Peru, Tanzania and Uganda” (delvedatabase.org).

factCheck.claim: In Tanzania, miners found licences hard to obtain and the licence term was seven years without guaranteed renewal, and a university trial gave retorts to 20 miners, 18 of whom used them for five months and recycled about 10 kilograms of mercury; in Ecuador a 1992 law legalised existing operations but credit did not develop; mercury was banned in Mongolia in 2008 but clandestine use continues.
factCheck.explanation: From the same 2012 analysis; conditions may have changed.
factCheck.reference: Hinton, J. (2012), as above.

the-bag-that-keeps-the-weevils-out.music: Warm northern drum and a steady flute; a bright tune when the clean grain is opened (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Hawawu, Hajia Asana and Mr Tia are invented. The research facts come from a 2018 IFPRI working paper on the cost-effectiveness of post-harvest technologies in Ghana: causes of loss (insects, mould, early or late harvest, grain not dry enough, selling at harvest); hermetic bags kept maize dry-weight loss below an average of 0.5 per cent over six months, cost about GH¢9 (US$2) in 2018 and gave better returns in Tamale over eight months; typical cabbage losses of about 60 per cent in Ghana; a zero energy cool chamber trial raised the saleable share after six days from 40 to 62 per cent, cost about US$1,040 and paid back after 18 uses.

The paper’s figures for maize losses of 10 to 30 per cent in ordinary storage are not Ghana-specific, and the story says so. Prices are from 2018 and the story tells learners to check current prices. Sums in the story use invented numbers, labelled as imaginary.

The story does not claim that a bag solves price problems or replaces drying; it shows an elder who tests one bag first and keeps the grain dry. It gives no medical advice about aflatoxin beyond naming it.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have an agricultural officer or post-harvest researcher check the descriptions of hermetic bags and the cool chamber, the 2018 figures and the dryness advice against current guidance.
Check the explanation of how a zero energy cool chamber keeps produce cool, because the paper’s summary gave results, not the mechanism.
Check the report-writing tip against the NaCCA English syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about reducing losses after harvest. It uses real trial figures with their dates and limits and models a short report.
learningGoals: Name two causes of post-harvest loss.
Explain how a hermetic bag protects grain and what the farmer must still do.
Write a short report with a heading, introduction, findings and recommendation.
beforeReading: Ask: where does food go between the farm and the plate? When can it be lost?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to say why the numbers are marked as imaginary.
afterReading: Write a report on how your family or school stores a food item.
Visit a market (with an adult) and ask how sellers keep vegetables fresh.

reflection: What food is wasted at home or at school, and how could it be saved?

mathsExtension.task: Suppose 100 kg of maize is worth GH¢300 and 20 per cent is lost. How much value is lost?

culturalNotes: Hawawu, Hajia Asana and Mr Tia are invented. The research facts come from a 2018 IFPRI working paper on the cost-effectiveness of post-harvest technologies in Ghana: causes of loss (insects, mould, early or late harvest, grain not dry enough, selling at harvest); hermetic bags kept maize dry-weight loss below an average of 0.5 per cent over six months, cost about GH¢9 (US$2) in 2018 and gave better returns in Tamale over eight months; typical cabbage losses of about 60 per cent in Ghana; a zero energy cool chamber trial raised the saleable share after six days from 40 to 62 per cent, cost about US$1,040 and paid back after 18 uses.

factCheck.claim: Hermetic PICS bags kept maize dry-weight loss below an average of 0.5 per cent over six months, cost about GH¢9 (US$2) for a 50 to 100 kg bag in 2018 and gave better returns than other options over eight months in Tamale; typical cabbage losses in Ghana are about 60 per cent; a zero energy cool chamber trial raised the saleable share after six days from 40 to 62 per cent, cost about US$1,040 and paid back after 18 uses.
factCheck.explanation: From a 2018 IFPRI working paper; trial results and prices from that period.
factCheck.reference: Baral, S. and Hoffmann, V. (2018), “Tackling Post Harvest Loss in Ghana: Cost-Effectiveness of Technologies”, IFPRI Working Paper (cgspace.cgiar.org).

factCheck.claim: Causes of post-harvest loss include insects (maize weevil, larger grain borer), mould and aflatoxin, harvesting too early or late, grain not dry enough, and selling immediately after harvest, which one study linked to a loss equal to 29.3 per cent of grain sales value.
factCheck.explanation: From the same paper; the last figure is from a study the paper cites.
factCheck.reference: Baral and Hoffmann (2018), as above.

culturalNotes: Enyonam, Auntie Comfort, Mr Gbeve and the market association are invented. whileReading: At page 4, ask learners to add one more honest question to the list.

culturalNotes: Enyonam, Auntie Comfort, Mr Gbeve and the market association are invented. The cold-room facts are from an IFPRI blog post (2018) quoting the founder of ColdHubs in Nigeria: solar-powered walk-in cold rooms in markets and on farms, run by two women each, about US$0.50 per crate per day, produce lasting up to 21 days instead of 2, five hubs saving nearly 5,800 tons of produce in two years, and more than 300 farmers, retailers and wholesalers nearly doubling monthly incomes. The article describes these as the founder’s reports; the story repeats that they are not independently checked.

The story does not claim that the same model works in Ghana. It lists the questions a Ghanaian market would need to answer (cost, ownership, repairs, trust, hygiene, roads, packaging, buyers). It names no real Ghanaian market, association or trader.

factCheck.claim: ColdHubs runs solar-powered cold rooms in markets and on farms in Nigeria, each run by two women, charging about US$0.50 per crate per day and extending produce life from about 2 to up to 21 days; five hubs reportedly saved nearly 5,800 tons of produce in two years and over 300 farmers, retailers and wholesalers reportedly nearly doubled their monthly incomes.

factCheck.reference: IFPRI, “ColdHubs: addressing a crucial problem, food loss in Nigeria, with solar-powered refrigeration” (ifpri.org, 2018).

narrationPlan.voice: A proud, slightly scornful boy’s voice for Kwao, softening as the story goes on; a calm, humorous young woman’s voice for Elinam

farming-is-not-for-failures.music: Bright, rhythmic afro-pop guitar with a light synth; a warm, hopeful tune at the descriptive paragraph (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Kwao, Elinam, Mrs Boampong and the school are invented. The examples of youth agriculture come from a March 2026 MyJoyOnline article: platforms such as AgroCenta and Farmerline give prices, weather and advice and help farmers sell directly; young farmers in the north use apps to plan planting; some young cocoa farmers use digital monitoring; a youth vegetable cooperative in the Ashanti Region supplies Accra supermarkets with cold-chain transport; young poultry farmers in the Volta Region use feed calculations. The article gives no proof for each example, so the story calls them reports. An 18 per cent rise in youth engagement quoted in the article could not be checked and is not used.

The oil palm figures come from a February 2023 news report of a municipal official’s briefing in the Birim Central Municipality: about 3,000 former small-scale illegal miners became oil palm farmers and 438,000 seedlings have been given out since 2020; the report notes that only people with farmland received seedlings, a beneficiary asked for a palm-processing factory, and long-term results are not yet known. The figures are not independently verified.

The mention of young people flying farm drones is based on news headlines about drone-pilot training for youth; details were not checked and the story gives no figures. The story shows farming as hard and uncertain, and does not suggest that a phone app guarantees profit.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have an agricultural extension officer check the examples of youth farming and the claim that platform features and fees differ, and replace any example that cannot be verified with a documented one.
Check the oil palm figures against the Minerals Commission or the municipal agriculture department, and check whether the project’s results have been assessed since 2023.
Check the descriptive-writing tip against the NaCCA English syllabus.

culturalNotes: Raphael, Fati, Mr Kyeremeh, Hudu and the club are invented, and the address in the letter is invented. Some members come from mining families; the story treats them with dignity and does not suggest that any of them is to blame.

The beekeeping facts come from a Ghana News Agency feature (3 August 2026) quoting beekeepers in the Volta Region: low start-up capital, no feed costs, use of marginal land, products (honey, beeswax, propolis, honeycomb), bush burning and tree felling as threats, and a lack of processing machinery and logistics. The story shares both the benefits and the limit.

The story does not give prices for hives, training or equipment because none were verified. The GH¢500 is an imaginary starting sum. The story says that nobody should handle a hive without training and protective clothing.

The facts in the story are simple: male frogs call to attract females; frogs eat insects, including mosquitoes; frog skin is thin and takes in water and air, which makes frogs sensitive to pollution. The story says that a loud pond is “healthy”, which is a simplification: many frogs are a sign of a living pond, but not proof that it is perfectly clean.

Safety: the children clean the edge with gloves and adults watching, and do not go into the water. Teachers should remind children that pond water and rubbish can carry germs and that they should wash their hands afterwards. They should not touch unknown animals.

teacherGuide.overview: A funny story that teaches simple tooth care. It uses cartoon “sugar bugs” to explain why sugar and brushing matter.
learningGoals: Say two things that help keep teeth healthy.
Say why too many sweets can hurt teeth.
Retell the story in order.
beforeReading: Ask: what do you do to keep your teeth clean?
whileReading: Wince on page 3 and cheer on page 8.
afterReading: Practise brushing on a model mouth with a big toothbrush.
Make a chart of “fruit and water” snacks.
discussion: Why did the nurse draw sugar bugs with party hats?
What can Iddi eat instead of sweets?
reflection: What is one habit you want to keep every day?

support: Use picture cards for brush, toothpaste, fruit and dentist.
stretch: Draw a tooth-care poster for the classroom door.

culturalNotes: Iddi, Nurse Manu and the family are invented. The story teaches the habits of brushing in the morning and at night, using a little toothpaste, eating fewer sweets and visiting a dentist.

“Sugar bugs” is a simple picture for the germs in the mouth that feed on sugar and make acid that damages teeth; the story says “tiny germs”. It does not suggest that sweets are bad in small amounts or that families who cannot afford a dentist are at fault; teachers should be sensitive to this.
Some families clean teeth in other ways; teachers should ask local health workers for advice and not criticise a family’s practices.
localiseThis: Ask a local health worker how families in your area look after their teeth and what a visit to the dentist costs. Do not shame any child for the state of their teeth.

factCheck.claim: Germs in the mouth feed on sugar and make acid that damages teeth; brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, eating less sugar and visiting a dentist help to protect teeth.
factCheck.explanation: Standard dental health guidance.
factCheck.reference: World Health Organization or Ghana Health Service oral health guidance (to verify).

learningGoals: Explain how a shadow is made.

culturalNotes: Lartekor and Auntie Efia are invented. The story is set during a power cut, which many families in Ghana have experienced. It does not blame anyone for power cuts and does not mention politics.

the-girl-who-asked-why.music: A curious, bouncy tune with a drum tap for every drop (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Ayeyi and Mr Marfo are invented. The story models a simple fair test: the same height, the same time, repeated three times, with results written in a table.

The science in the story is simple and well known: a stone and a pencil dropped together land at almost the same time because the air pushes very little on both; a flat sheet of paper falls more slowly than a crumpled ball because air pushes up on it more. The story does not claim that all objects fall at the same speed in all cases, and it says that shape matters as well as weight.
Safety: the test is done on a soft patch of sand, with small objects, at a low height. Teachers should make sure children do not drop anything from a height or from windows.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have a science teacher check the statements about falling objects and air resistance and the description of a fair test for this age group.
Check that the safety advice is clear and the experiment is safe in a school yard.

teacherGuide.overview: A chant for the brushing habit. Form: four couplets. Rhyming pairs: light/right, row/slow, done/one, care/share. It teaches a daily habit and rhyme.

Show how to brush gently.
Spot rhymes.
beforeReading: Ask: who has a toothbrush? When do you use it?
whileReading: Mime brushing as you chant.
afterReading: Draw a happy tooth and a sad tooth.

culturalNotes: Many families also clean teeth with a chewing stick. This chant uses a toothbrush; teachers may add other safe cleaning methods that families use.

factCheck.claim: Brush, Brush, Brush (a tooth-brushing chant)

teacherGuide.overview: A tug-of-war chant. Form: four couplets. Rhyming pairs: rope/hope, one/done, not/spot, done/fun. It teaches teamwork and good sportsmanship.
learningGoals: Work as a team.
Lose and win well.
Spot rhymes.
beforeReading: Talk about how a team works together.
whileReading: Use a call-and-response beat.
afterReading: Play with a thick rope on a flat grassy area, with adults supervising and teams of similar size.
discussion: Why shake hands after a game?
reflection: How can you help your team?

support: Use clapping instead of pulling for children who need a quiet role.
stretch: Write a chant for another team game.

culturalNotes: Tug of war is a common sports-day event in Ghanaian schools. The chant is original.
localiseThis: Use the real sports-day rules of your school.
Never wrap the rope around hands or arms.

teacherGuide.overview: A kite rhyme with a safety message. Form: four couplets. Rhyming pairs: blue/flew, string/thing, high/by, play/day. It teaches safe play and rhyme.
learningGoals: Name where it is safe to fly a kite.
Say why wires are dangerous.
Spot rhymes.
beforeReading: Ask: where have you seen wires? Why should we stay away?
whileReading: Slow down at the safety page.
afterReading: Make a kite from paper and sticks and fly it in an open field away from wires, with an adult, on a dry day.
discussion: What should you do if a kite gets caught on a wire?
reflection: Which safety rule will you remember?

support: Use pictures of safe and unsafe places and sort them.
stretch: Write a safety poster for kite flyers.

culturalNotes: Kite flying is a popular harmattan pastime in many places. The safety message is general and is also taught by electricity companies.
localiseThis: Use the local fields children know. If a kite gets caught on a wire, leave it and tell an adult. Never climb to get it.

factCheck.claim: Kites should be flown in open fields on dry days, far from overhead power lines and roads, and never retrieved from wires.
factCheck.explanation: Overhead electrical lines carry dangerous current; kite strings or climbing near wires can cause electric shock.
factCheck.reference: Confirm wire-safety advice with the local electricity company (e.g. Electricity Company of Ghana public safety guidance).

learningGoals: Say what to do if a ball rolls toward a road.
Ask an adult for help.
Say thank you.
beforeReading: Ask: where is a safe place to play ball?
whileReading: Stop sharply on the word Stop and let children freeze.
afterReading: Play a freeze game: bounce, then stop on a signal.
discussion: Whom can you ask for help?
reflection: Where is your safe play place?

support: Act the story with a soft ball and a taped line.
stretch: Draw a safe play area with a fence.

culturalNotes: Road safety matters for children in towns and villages across Ghana. The rhyme is original.
localiseThis: Name the real safe play places near the school. Make sure each child knows who the nearest adult is.
